input.question: How is it that now matter how full a person gets, there are some foods like French fries where a person can always seem to have room for one more?
input.ground_truth: Generalising, but it's because the body has two broad drivers of feeding: * direct nutrient deficit (ie, you need energy - or at least, your body thinks you need energy!) * pleasurable food consumption - also known as [hedonic hunger](_URL_1_). Hedonic hunger probably primarily evolved to promote the consumption of high-energy foods even if you are 'full', to put on more fat and increase resistance to famine. French fries are high in fat, salt and easily digestible carbohydrates - a perfect food to put on that survival weight! [This review](_URL_0_) goes over the evolution of hedonic hunger in quite an easy to understand fashion.

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: How is it that now matter how full a person gets, there are some foods like French fries where a person can always seem to have room for one more?

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine your tummy is like a toy box. When you eat, you put toys (the food) inside the box. Some toys, like soft blocks (maybe like mashed potatoes or bread), fill up the box really fast. But other toys, like curly straws or long, thin toys (like French fries), don’t take up as much space even if you have a lot of them.

Also, French fries are fun and tasty, so your brain says, “Let’s have one more!” even when your tummy is almost full. That’s why sometimes, even if you’re full, you can still eat one more French fry!
